s: My purpose in coming here was only to show the full sympathy I feel with the purpose of the meeting, without any intention of speaking; but being asked to do so, I cannot refrain, for love's sake, from saying a few words.
One point has struck me particularly, concerning the Headship of our adorable Lord Jesus.
It is the will of that blessed One that His disciples should love one another, and be united together in heart and affection.

If, then, it is the will of Him without whom we must perish eternally, who poured out His soul to death for our life, and stooped so low that we might share His throne, that we should love one another and be united as His disciples, is it not fitting for us, in love and gratitude, to obey?
What are the great hindrances to brotherly love and unity?

Self-satisfaction, high-mindedness, pride, and thinking that we know more than others; but if, by God's grace, we are enabled to subdue these evil tendencies, and to love our fellow believer and be united to him, we shall perhaps see that if in one thing we have more grace or knowledge than he, yet in four or five, or ten points he has more than we.
Who am I that I should despise my brother?
What do I have that I have not received?
If I have more grace (though that is yet to be questioned), I received it from my Lord.
If I have more knowledge (though that is still questionable), do I owe it to my own mind?
How does it come?
It is by the grace of God that I know more than my fellow believer.

If, then, we are what we are by the grace of God, so that every particle of power over sin, of heavenly-mindedness, of desire to act according to the Holy Scriptures, becomes ours because it pleased God, in the riches of His grace, to bless us in this way, who are we that we should look down on a brother because there are degrees of ignorance or spiritual weakness in a fellow disciple?
Jesus is our Head.
It is His will that we should love one another.
In gratitude to that blessed One, who laid down His life that I might be saved, let me obey; and if I find that pride keeps me from it, let me seek grace to subdue it.
“We who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.”
When we meet a brother who is weak in grace or knowledge, our natural tendency is to say, “Oh, he is a weak one.”
The carnal mind says, “Put him aside.”
But the Word of the blessed Lord says, “Bear the infirmities of the weak.”
If I am strong, let me prove my strength by putting my shoulder to the burden.
If I cannot bear with the weakness of my brother, it is plain proof that I am a weak one myself.
Why have we received grace?
That we may help along our weaker or less instructed brother—that in helping others we may bring glory to God.
I think it may not be unprofitable to refer to one thing in my own experience.

When I began, thirty-four years ago, as a young servant of Christ, to labor in the Word in this country, having just received certain blessed truths—such as the coming of the Lord, and others—my natural tendency was to look down on those who did not see them.
Thirty-four years have passed since then.

By God's grace I hold those blessed truths as firmly as ever, and maintain them as strongly; but as to my conduct toward other disciples who do not agree with me on these points, there is a difference now.
The attitude of the young servant of Christ was to say, “Stand aloof!”—to regard them as very little instructed.
What was the result?
Was it peace and joy in the Holy Spirit?
Did I imitate Him who bore with the ignorance of His disciples?
No; it was anything but an imitation of Jesus, and the result was anything but peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
By the help of God I am now, and have been for more than twenty years, of a different mind, without sacrificing one particle of those truths which I received in the year 1829.
My aim now is to bear with those who may be less instructed; and in the measure in which I am able to follow the example of my adorable Lord, the result is peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
I affectionately and earnestly urge my dear fellow believers, especially the young, to ponder this.
Pray to be kept from a spirit of high-mindedness.
What you have and are, you have and are by the grace of God, and that should lead you to deal tenderly with your fellow disciples.
It is often said that for the sake of peace and union we should not be very particular about certain parts of truth, but should keep them back and treat them as matters of no importance.
I humbly state that I entirely differ from this view; for I do not see that such union is of a real, lasting, or Scriptural character.

If it is truth, it is dear to the heart of Jesus—we are instructed in it by the blessed Spirit—it is found in God's book; it is therefore of great value and must be considered worthy of being carefully and jealously guarded.
We are therefore not at liberty to esteem lightly, undervalue, or keep in the background (much less give up) the truth, even for the sake of union.
We must buy the truth at any cost, but we ought not to sell it at any price, not even for our liberty or our life.

Yet while we hold fast the truth, all the truth in which we consider we have been instructed from the Holy Scriptures, we must always remember that it is not the degree of knowledge that believers have attained which should unite them, but the common spiritual life they have in Jesus: that they are purchased by the blood of Jesus; members of the same family; going to the Father's house—soon to be all there; and by reason of the common life they have, brethren should dwell together in unity.
It is the will of the Father, and of that blessed One who laid down His life for us, that we should love one another.
But it may be asked, Is it possible that brethren who differ in this and that can be united together?
They can. In the three orphan houses and six schools under my direction there are sixty teachers and other helpers.

These are found to belong to the Church of England, the Presbyterians, the Independents, the Baptists of close communion and of open communion, the Wesleyans of the Conference and of the Free Church parties, and the so-called “Brethren.”
All these, though from different bodies of saints, are united together in this one object of laboring for Christ.
During the many years we have been engaged in this way, I have never known any discord to arise because of such differences.
This does not arise from a sort of latitudinarianism in myself, but because, while holding firmly to my own convictions, I have not required uniformity in these laborers.
In engaging my helpers, it is indispensable that they belong to the Head, that they hold fast the blessed Son of God.
This settled, I never ask what denomination they belong to.
This is not brought forward boastfully, but to magnify the grace of God.
It is often said that things are stated on the platform which cannot possibly be carried out in practical life.

I maintain that this loving one another must be possible, because it is commanded by God; and especially may the beloved brethren in Christ who have gathered together these saints before me be assured that it is possible to do everything that is according to the will of God.
It must be possible to do what God has commanded.
And let us not think that it is an extraordinary and high degree of attainment for Christians to walk together in love.
The least instructed saints should be found willing to love, though they may not agree on every point.
“As far as we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule.”

On many things we are agreed, and walking together in this way, holding in our hearts the headship of Jesus, it is certain that we shall make progress; “and if in anything you are otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this to you.”
Do not say of anything, “I shall never understand this.”
That is entirely a mistake.
As to the things of God, despair of nothing.
Never make agreement about particular points of truth the basis of union.
If my brethren differ from me, I must not say, “It is a matter of no importance”; neither should I say, “I shall never know this or that truth,” which may not yet have been revealed to me.

Let there be more prayer, more study of the Word, more humility, more acting out of what we already know; in this way we shall be more united together, not only in love, but in one mind and in one judgment.
There will be no difference in heaven.
There all are of one mind.
Let us aim at the heavenly condition.
More patience and more faith will bring us further on in blessing.
May God grant it to this assembly for the sake of Jesus!

The two great objects of our salvation are—first, primarily and especially, that God may be glorified; and secondly, at the same time, that His children may be conformed to the image of His dear Son, in order to ensure their eternal happiness.
They could not possibly be happy even in heaven unless they were conformed in this way.
The work begins here, and will be completed when we are with the Lord; not until then shall we be perfectly conformed to the image of Christ.

This is the blessed, glorious prospect of all who believe in the Lord Jesus—that a day is coming when, their will being swallowed up in the will of God, and having no will of their own, God will only have to present His blessed will to them, and instantly, in their inmost souls, they will respond.
For this we have been laid hold of by God in Christ Jesus.

It is not only true that we shall be perfectly free from pain, sickness, and this corruptible body, and have a glorified body; but also that the day is coming when we shall be perfectly like Jesus in holiness, when we shall have no mind of our own, when the will of God will only need to be presented to us and at once we shall act accordingly.
God is the Author of salvation, and this salvation is to be obtained entirely by way of grace.
Men cannot, in the least degree, help God in obtaining it.
Salvation is entirely from God, bestowed by way of grace through Jesus Christ, His only begotten Son, whom He wounded, bruised, and punished in our place and stead.
Jesus, having given Himself to be our substitute, was punished for us.
“The Lord has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.”
And all that is required of us is to accept or believe in Him, to accept the salvation which He gives us freely.

If, therefore, anyone who feels himself to be a sinner asks, “How shall I get this precious salvation?” the Word of God replies, “Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ” (that is, trust in the Lord Jesus Christ), “and you shall be saved.”
We must give no other answer than the one the Apostle Paul gave to the Philippian jailer.

I would say to my dear fellow sinner: Trust in—depend on—receive what Jesus has obtained for you; if you will leave your own merits and goodness, and trust entirely in Christ, this very moment you shall receive forgiveness of sins.
The faith in Jesus which obtains forgiveness brings you near to God, removes the enmity which existed between you and God, and gives peace to your soul.
The primary object of salvation—the glory of God—is accomplished in every sinner saved in this way.
Then as to the one who is saved.
Having been laid hold of by God in Christ Jesus, you will ultimately be conformed to the image of Christ, and be perfectly happy and holy.
Especially will this holiness be shown in the perfection of your love.
God is love, and you will be made perfect in love.
This leads to a word of practical application concerning our present meeting.
While we are not yet in heaven, we are not yet conformed to the image of God's dear Son—we are not perfect in love now.
But this perfect love is to be aimed at and sought after.
We are assembled now in order that our hearts may be drawn together in love.
Though not yet perfect in love, we are to aim at that for which we have been laid hold of by God in Christ Jesus.
We ought to love one another in spite of the weaknesses and infirmities we see in one another.
My brethren have their infirmities, and I have my infirmities; God knows them all, and He alone can estimate which are the greater.
That is not a question for us.
Believing in Jesus, we have one common life; the precious blood of Jesus has purchased us; we are the children of God by faith as surely as we trust in Him for salvation.
As children, then, of the same Father, as brothers and sisters of the same heavenly family, notwithstanding our weaknesses, we ought to love one another and bear with each other's infirmities.
With any who live in sin, or who, though professing to be disciples of Christ, renounce the foundations of our most holy faith, there can be no fellowship.
Loyalty to our Lord will compel us to stand aloof from such, painful though it may be.
But all true disciples we are bound, in loyalty to our Head, to love as such, and to bear with their infirmities and weaknesses.
If I see a little more clearly concerning this or that part of God's truth than my brother does, is that any reason why I should stand aloof from him?
If I have been better instructed, I am to use this knowledge not to exalt myself, not to praise myself, but for my fellow disciple, and to instruct him in a kind and loving way.
And if that brother will not receive my instruction, still I am not to stand aloof from him, but to pray for him, and still to bear with my brother for the sake of Him who bears with my infirmities.
Am I myself fully instructed?
No! A day is coming when I shall know even as I am known.
But that day has not yet come.

If I have a little more knowledge than my fellow disciple, still I know only in part, and I am what I am by the grace of God; and that very superiority of knowledge is given (if I have it—I may be mistaken in supposing I have more) so that I may use it for the benefit of my less instructed and weaker brother.
If I have strength, let me prove it by putting my shoulder beneath the burden.
The strong are to bear the infirmities of the weak, and if I am unable to do that, it is plain proof that I am a weak one myself, and have no ground to complain of the weaknesses of my brethren.
All, to a greater or lesser degree, are still weak, still uninstructed; none has room for boasting.
We are all debtors to the grace of God, and should therefore praise more abundantly, walk more humbly, and seek more fully to bear one another's burdens.
Only a little while, and the blessed Jesus will come again, so that where He is we may be also.
In the meantime, let us love one another.
Love is of God.
God is love; and he who loves most is most like God.
All the members of the heavenly family should remember the precious blood that bought them, and love one another while on the way to their Father's house.
It was in July 1829 that I first became acquainted with Mr. Craik.

What drew me to him was not that we were both nearly twenty-four years of age at that time; nor was it that we had both had a university education; nor was it that we were both, at that time, pursuing the study of the Hebrew language with great love and earnestness; nor was it even that both of us had been brought to the knowledge of the Lord Jesus at about the same time, while at the university; but what it was that drew me to him will be seen in what follows.
In May 1829, soon after my arrival in England, I was taken very ill.
My desire then was very strong to depart, so that I might be with my Lord, whom I adore, who had loved me and given Himself for me, the great sinner.

It pleased God, however, contrary to my expectation, and especially contrary to my desire, to begin to restore me; and in order to complete my recovery, I was medically advised to leave London for a change of air.
In submission to the will of God I went to Teignmouth; for although the state of heart I was in desired no prolonging of life, I still considered it my duty to use this means.
While at Teignmouth, I became acquainted with Mr. Craik, and his warmth of heart toward the Lord drew me to him.
It was this that attracted me.
As I stayed only a few weeks at Teignmouth, I saw comparatively little of him; but in January 1830 I returned to Teignmouth, and from then on I lived there.

We were now drawn together more fully; for between July 1829 and January 1830 I had seen the leading truths connected with the second coming of our Lord Jesus; I had grasped the all-sufficiency of the Holy Scriptures as our rule, and of the Holy Spirit as our teacher; I had seen clearly the precious doctrines of the grace of God, in which I had been uninstructed for nearly four years after my conversion; and I had learned the heavenly calling of the Church of Christ, and the resulting position of the believer in this world.

As these very truths so greatly occupied Mr. Craik’s heart also, we were now soon drawn closely together; and from that time until the day he fell asleep in Jesus, our friendship was intimate and unbroken for thirty-six years.

The reader will learn from the memoir itself that we remained laboring in the Word in the same locality in Devonshire for about two years and three months; and then, in a very marked way, we were both led at the same time to Bristol, where we have labored together for more than thirty-three years.
It has often been observed how remarkable it was that we should have labored together so harmoniously for so many years, and that this should have continued to the very last.
Now, as I write this introduction for the reader’s profit, I will dwell a little on this point.
It was not because Mr. Craik had no mind of his own and therefore habitually submitted to my judgment; nor was it because I blindly followed him, having no judgment of my own.

All our Christian friends who knew us were well aware that this was not at all the case; but the reasons were these: When in the year 1832 I saw how some preferred my beloved friend’s ministry to my own, I determined, in the strength of God, to rejoice in this instead of envying him.
I said, with John the Baptist, “A man can receive nothing unless it is given him from heaven” (John 3:27).
This resisting of the devil kept our hearts from being separated.
But this was not all.
From that time God also honored me in the ministry of the Word, and greatly so; this is mentioned only to show how a double blessing followed my resisting the devil.

But when, from the beginning of 1839 onward, it pleased the Lord to condescend to bestow such abundant honor on me as He did in connection with the Orphan Houses and the other objects of the Scriptural Knowledge Institution for Home and Abroad, the temptation ran the other way, especially as this work was extended more and more, and the blessing of God resting on it became greater and greater.
Then my beloved friend, for his part, speaking after the manner of men, had cause for envy.
But how was it in reality?
There were few, if any, who more truly rejoiced in all the honor the Lord condescended to put on me than my friend did.
Still, this was not all.

This in particular must be added: whatever the spiritual infirmities of my friend or of myself were, there was given to us, throughout the whole thirty-six years of our friendship, an honest purpose to live to God, not to ourselves; to please Him, and not ourselves; and so it came about that our friendship remained unbroken to the end, even though the temptations to alienation of heart, humanly speaking, increased more and more instead of decreasing.

Our natural makeup of mind and temperament was very different, and yet we had to work together, while about 2,500 believers have been received into fellowship since we first came to Bristol, and while in recent years nearly 1,000 believers have been in fellowship in the church meeting at Bethesda and Salem chapels, among whom we labored.
Who, then, can doubt the difficulty that constantly stood in the way of this continuance of love and union? But there was help to be found in God, and we found it to the end.
This is how we parted when I saw my dear friend for the last time.

After I had kissed him, when I intended to go, he, being too weak to converse any more, said, “Sit down,” and also asked Mrs. Craik to sit down, so that he might look at us, though he could not converse.
So I sat there silently for a while, and then left.
This was our last meeting.
The next day I caught a cold and was kept at home for several days, during which time my dear friend fell asleep.

The reader will see from the memoir that Mr. Craik had very superior powers of mind; but what made him especially lovely in my estimation were the following features of his character and spiritual attainments:
1. He was very affectionate.
2. Like Nathanael of old, he was truly without deceit.
3. He was particularly conscientious.
Whatever his weakness or failing in any respect, you could be sure that he acted conscientiously.
He did what he did because he thought it right.
Our views concerning certain courses of action differed materially, but I always came back to this: My friend is conscientious; if he only saw as I did, he would surely act differently.
4. Though endowed by God with such great mental powers, he did not use them to make a name among men, nor to be admired by men, but to throw light on the Holy Scriptures and to set forth the truth.

As a striking proof of his humility, and of how far he was from seeking the honor of men, I mention the following: In the year 1849 Professor Alexander indicated to him, in the name of the University of St Andrews, that it was intended to confer on him the degree of Doctor of Divinity, or of Doctor of Canon and Civil Law.
He courteously declined this honor, but recommended for the degree a Christian gentleman who had labored much in biblical literature, as it might be of great use to him as an author.

The latter was done, and the degree of LL.D. was conferred on this gentleman. Some years ago the same university repeated to Mr. Craik their former proposal and desire, and a second time my friend humbly declined the honor.

Truly this is a striking proof that, whatever momentary failings to the contrary there may have been, he was steadfastly purposed in his heart not to seek the honor that comes from man, but to commend himself to God as His servant.
5. Mr. Craik showed great sympathy to those who were in trial and affliction: his affectionate heart felt deeply for the sufferings of others.
6. Mr. Craik was eminently a man of prayer, and a man given to the study of the Word of God.

Such prayerfulness regarding the Holy Scriptures, such true digging into the Word as for hidden treasures, such meditation on the Word as he was given to, I never knew to be surpassed by any servant of Christ.

The chief loss that the Church of Christ at large has sustained in his removal is not merely that he was a lovely, amiable, truly spiritually minded Christian to all who knew him intimately, and an earnest, devoted preacher of the Lord Jesus; but that he was one who had truly studied the oracles of God on his knees, with great diligence.

Among all the thousands of believers whom I know, there is none whose judgment on any part of truth I would have valued more than that of my departed friend, because of his great caution, his prayerfulness, his diligence in comparing Scripture with Scripture, his humility of soul, his very considerable knowledge of Greek and Hebrew, and his habit of reading the Scriptures in their original languages.

Concerning Mr. Craik’s health, as one who knew him so intimately and so long, I must state that when he was about forty years old he looked far healthier than when I first knew him at twenty-four years of age, and this was even more the case when he was about fifty.
He was never strong, and, like many men of great mind, he was not careful enough to make the best of the health and strength he had.
He would generally eat rapidly and, though suffering from weak digestion, neglect to chew his food properly.
Moreover, when he felt fairly well, he would forget his constitutional weakness and labor mentally beyond his strength.

This is not stated to cast any blame on that excellent man who is no longer among us, but his friend states it as a warning to his fellow believers; for life, health, and strength of body or mind are entrusted to us as precious talents to be used for God.

This lack of habitually acting with caution regarding his health, and his overtaxing of his mind, no doubt produced at certain times a measure of nervous depression, of which the reader will find indications in his diary, and which makes Mr. Craik appear almost to be a different man from what he was known to be in his ordinary public life, in which he generally showed great cheerfulness.
Having referred to his health, I cannot help adding that it is my full conviction that my friend’s constitutional weakness was intended by God as a special blessing to him.

Though Mr. Craik was a very humble man, and though it was his earnest and habitual desire to use his mental powers for the glory of God, yet no one could know him intimately without being aware that his natural tendency was to pursue the cultivation of his mind with too great an earnestness and natural fondness, which, but for his weak constitution, might have become a great snare to his inner man.
As a check, therefore, the Lord so mercifully gave him this powerful mind together with a weak body, so that he might not indulge too much in the cultivation of his mental powers.
I add this further with regard to his health.
I never knew anyone who by constitution shrank from suffering as much as he did.
He often spoke to me on this subject.
And yet this very man was, for nearly seven months before his death, not only a very great sufferer, but was also greatly sustained under his great sufferings.

On Christmas Day 1865, as I sat at his bedside longer than usual, because I had more time than I generally did, I suddenly remembered what he had so often spoken to me about, and then told him that now the strength of the Lord was made manifest in his constitutional shrinking from pain and suffering.
He saw it and acknowledged it.
And truly the Lord greatly sustained His suffering servant, and did so to the end.
Without complaining he passed through his sufferings, though he prayed and longed to be delivered from them.
And at last he was delivered.
Peacefully leaning on Jesus, he fell asleep.
His poor friend who writes this remains.
For now the Lord allows me to serve Him on earth.
Pray, Christian reader, that whether this time is long or short, I may be enabled to spend it truly to the honor of God.
The occasion that gave rise to this letter was this: Philemon, who lived at Colosse (for this can plainly be seen from the last chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Colossians.
The letter to the church at Colosse was written at the same time as this letter to Philemon.

Onesimus and another brother were the bearers of the letter to the church at Colosse and of this private letter to Philemon)—Philemon, who lived at Colosse, had a slave by the name of Onesimus, and this slave, in his ungodly state, ran away from his master Philemon, and in the providence of God, as we say, he comes to Rome.
Rome was the greatest place in the whole world at that time.
In all probability this slave said to himself, “If I could get to Rome, what prospects there would be before me.”
This may have occurred to him after he left his master.
He wanders on from Asia Minor to Rome with bright prospects before him.
“Oh, what pleasures I shall have in Rome; what sights I shall see in Rome; what companionship I shall meet with in Rome!”
No doubt some such thoughts passed through his mind.
And what happened in Rome?
He was converted. So God allows men to go their own way; so God allows men to follow the desires of their own heart, and if they could, they would run still farther and farther away from Him.
But God says, “Thus far you shall go, and no farther.”

Many have gone to London and to other places, not to get good for their souls, but in the service of the devil; but God laid hold of them there, in the very way they least expected, and converted them.
Again, Onesimus might have come to Rome and never seen Paul.

He might have spent fifty years in Rome and never seen Paul; but God has purposes of grace and mercy toward him, and in His good providence He orders it so that he falls in with Paul, so that he must become acquainted with this Paul.
And who was Paul at this time in Rome?
Not a great man in the eyes of the world.
Truly a great man in one sense, and yet in the greatest obscurity in another sense.
Paul was at this time a prisoner for the gospel’s sake.
Paul did not walk about in the marketplace, the Forum, where the great and wealthy of the capital gathered.

He was in prison, with a soldier guarding him, and yet God so orders it that this runaway slave must fall in with Paul, and that Paul shall become a blessed instrument in the hands of God for the conversion of his soul.
How full of encouragement this should be to us all!

Some have dear ones who are far from Christ—fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, and other relatives—and many of them are apparently getting farther and farther from God, caring less and less about the things of God and more and more about the things of this world.
Go on, beloved in Christ, believingly and patiently bringing their cases before the Lord, and you will yet have the joy of finding that your prayers have not been in vain.

There is every reason to believe that Philemon, the godly master of this slave, was concerned about his spiritual welfare; but all seems lost when this slave runs away, and yet God follows him and lays hold of him at the very time when you and I would least have thought he would be brought to the Lord.
Let us read and meditate on this letter to Philemon.
Verse 1: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon our dearly beloved and fellow worker.”
He regarded this Philemon as one who labored with him in the gospel.
He speaks of him and treats him as a fellow worker.

Verse 2: “And to our beloved Apphia (the wife of Philemon), and to Archippus our fellow soldier (this Archippus was a brother who labored in the word and doctrine at Colosse), and to the church in your house.”
The house of Archippus was the meeting place of the church, for at that time churches and chapels were not built, but they met in private houses or in places that were fitted up for the purpose.
We have an instance of this in the twentieth chapter of Acts, where Paul was preaching in an upper room.
It was not the aim of the disciples to have costly buildings resembling the temple at Jerusalem.
The first hundred and twenty met in an upper room.
So here the church at Colosse had the house of Philemon as its meeting place.
Verse 3: “Grace to you.”
You notice how this comes in in the various letters addressed to the churches, and there must be a reason for it.
It is not a mere common phrase that is brought in.
The reason seems to be this: we need to be reminded that grace has been bestowed on us by God through Christ Jesus, and that He is willing to bestow more and more blessing.
And so also we need to be reminded continually of the fact that we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

I am now speaking only to those who trust in the Lord Jesus Christ—who, having passed sentence on themselves and condemned themselves in the sight of God as guilty sinners, are trusting in the atoning death of the Lord Jesus Christ as the one ground of acceptance before God.

Verses 4–7: “I thank my God, making mention of you always in my prayers, hearing of your love and faith, which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all saints; that the communication of your faith may become effective by the acknowledging of every good thing which is in you in Christ Jesus.
For we have great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints are refreshed by you, brother.”
This is what the apostle Paul writes regarding the spiritual state of Philemon, and a high commendation it is—a most blessed man of God he was; and yet someone says, “He had slaves!”
Yes, he had slaves.
But we must always keep this before us: having slaves at that time was not connected with such awful cruelty as the slavery of modern days.
Many of these people were idolaters, and there were many things connected with slavery that were quite wrong.
Yet, ordinarily speaking, we have no reason to believe that there were the cruelties of the slaveholders of modern days.

In most of the instances where we read the word “servant,” it means slave—those who belonged to the master; but in not one single instance is there a hint given such as, “How wicked you are, how cruel and abominable your conduct!”

If the love of Christ constrained them to set all free, the apostles would have rejoiced in it; and when these slaves had the opportunity of becoming free, they were to accept it thankfully and not reject it.
The apostle Paul commends Philemon on account of the blessed spiritual state he was in.
He says, “I thank my God,” and this particularly with reference to the fifth verse, “hearing of your love and faith.”
This was a subject for praise and thanksgiving in Paul’s heart with regard to Philemon.
This is rather a remarkable expression, “faith and love toward the saints.”
You can see what it means that he had love; but what is the meaning of this, that he had faith toward the saints?
Have you ever thought about this?
It is deeply important that we seek to search into the meaning of what we read in the Divine testimony.
The meaning of it is evidently this: looking on them with faith, seeing in them that they are the children of God, and treating them as such—as the children of God.
Whenever we are enabled to look on one another as the children of God, whenever we are enabled to see Christ in one another, that is exercising faith toward one another.
He also prayed that God would help him further, and from this we should gather instruction: as Paul prayed for Philemon, so we should pray for each other.
This was the subject of his prayer: “that the communication of your faith may become effective by the acknowledging of every good thing which is in you in Christ Jesus.”

In other words, this means: My dear Philemon, I pray that you, having received faith, may go on; that this may energize you, may become effective in you, and give you still further and further strength to acknowledge everything that is good in any of the saints.
And he adds this to his praise in the seventh verse: “For we have great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints are refreshed by you, brother.”
What a high commendation of this dear man!

Evidently he was one in a position of comparative wealth and prosperity, and Paul says, “we have great joy,” because on account of the holy, godly walk of this blessed man of God, Philemon, the hearts of the saints were refreshed.
Do we, the children of God, aim at this—namely, that we become a spiritual refreshment to the saints, that the saints are refreshed by our godly life?
This is what we must aim at.

When we give way to our natural tendencies, to our temper, and to other things that are hateful to God, we do not strengthen the hands of our fellow disciples; but when we seek to do the things that are according to the mind of God, we strengthen each other’s hands in God.
In bringing glory to God, we also help along the life and conduct of other children of God.
It is just as with an army: if one regiment acquits itself well, the other regiments are strengthened by it; and if one regiment turns its back on the enemy, the other regiments are weakened by it.
So it is with the Church of God.

Verses 8–14: “Therefore, though I could be very bold in Christ to order you to do what is proper, yet for love’s sake I rather plead with you, being such a one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

I plead with you for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my chains, who in time past was unprofitable to you, but now is profitable to you and to me; whom I have sent back. You therefore receive him, that is, my own heart. I would have kept him with me, so that in your place he might have ministered to me in the bonds of the gospel; but without your consent I would do nothing, so that your good deed would not be as it were of necessity, but willingly.”
An exquisite statement this, and of the deepest importance.
In brief it was just this: Onesimus was converted; Paul was a prisoner in chains for the gospel.
What a comfort this good man would have been in waiting on him!
He longed to have someone to wait on him.
Paul might have said, “This Onesimus is my son in the faith, and therefore I shall simply act as I have a right to act; I will just keep him and let him wait on me.”
He might have said, “I am an apostle, and for the gospel’s sake I am here in prison, and it is right and fitting that my child in the faith should wait on me.”
Not so, not so.
This was not the mind of Christ, and this blessed man of God sought to act according to the mind of Christ.

He might have said, “I am an aged servant of Christ, an aged apostle, and I have labored more abundantly than any of them; and since this runaway slave has been converted through me, it is quite right that I should have him to wait on me.”
Not so, because this would be by constraint.
He would not know whether it was done willingly and cheerfully on Philemon’s part.
He desired that this man of God might do what he did cheerfully and willingly.
Oh, how deeply important it is to keep this before us!
The principle is just this.

Suppose someone said, “Now I am in great need, and so-and-so is my brother in Christ, and so-and-so has plenty of money, and he ought to give to me because I am a poor brother; he is bound by the word of God to do it, and I have a right simply to demand it of him.”
Is this the mind of Christ?
It is the mind of the flesh, and not the mind of Christ.
You never find such an instance on the part of a man of God in the epistles or the gospels.

It is quite true that whoever has this world’s goods, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart of compassion, cannot have the love of God in him; but it is also true, on the other hand, that it is unbecoming for a poor brother to insist on it.
The apostle Paul could have insisted on his rights, but he did not do so.
“Who in time past was unprofitable to you.”
This brings out the character of Onesimus: a good-for-nothing man, a bad fellow.
Philemon had lost nothing.
“But now profitable to you and to me.”
Because he was a child of God, a brother in Christ, a member of the body.
That brings out another deeply important principle.
There is no child of God who is not of some good.
Someone might say, “Here is a very ignorant person who cannot put two letters together; what good is such a one to the Church of Christ?”
If in no other way, then by giving others the opportunity to exercise grace.
Here is one who is helplessly confined to his bed year after year.
That person can pray; that person can still show the mind of Christ to anyone who comes to see him.
And even if none of these things were so, such people still give those who are in health and strength the opportunity to show love to them.
We should always look on one another as precious in the sight of Christ.
Our natural tendency is this: to see the old Adam in one another, to see the failings and shortcomings in one another; and the result is misery to one another and dishonor to God.
O beloved in Christ, let us aim to see Christ in one another.
Onesimus was profitable to the chief of the apostles—just think of this!
He could not be a useless one, because he was a member of the body of Christ, and Christ can have no member of His body who is altogether useless.
“You therefore receive him, that is, my own heart.”
Philemon was to receive him as if Paul himself had come to him.
And oh, how would Paul have been received?
“O beloved brother Paul, how glad I am to see you here again!” he would say, falling on his neck and kissing him many times.

Now Paul says, “Just as you would have received me if I were to come, so, beloved Philemon, receive this runaway slave, because he is your brother in Christ, and you will have to spend a happy eternity with him.”
“But without your consent I would do nothing.”
But I must first know that this pleases you, that you are satisfied with it, that this is according to your wish and will.
How deeply important it is to keep this before us in the Divine life, that we show the mind of Christ.
Just as that blessed One did not seek to please Himself, but to be the servant of others, so we must imitate that blessed One.
“For perhaps he departed for a season for this reason, that you should receive him forever.” “Forever”—never to be separated any more.
And that brings before us the precious truth that the disciples of the Lord Jesus are bound together for eternity, are knit together for eternity.
And that, you see, is so precious.
There may come separation by distance, there may come separation by death; ah, but it is only in appearance.
We are bound together in the bonds of love, not for time only, but for eternity.
All the poor sinners who rest on the atoning death of the Lord Jesus form one holy, happy, blessed family for eternity, and there will be no separation for eternity.
Do we belong to that family?
Do we believe in the Lord Jesus?
How many among us belong to the heavenly family?
How many have decided yet?
Put this question to yourselves, you dear young men, you dear girls from the Orphan Houses, and all who are present here.
Oh, the blessedness of belonging to the heavenly family!
Oh, the blessedness of belonging to the members of Christ!
Then let come what may—one in Christ, and one in Christ forever!

“Who forgives all your iniquities; who heals all your diseases; who redeems your life from destruction; who crowns you with lovingkindness and tender mercies; who satisfies your mouth with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.”—Psalm 103:3–5
In this Psalm, which I read to you, we should particularly notice the stress the Psalmist lays on praise: “Bless the Lord (or Jehovah), O my soul, and all that is within me.”
His soul is engaged in the service.
All!—the affections of his heart, the powers of his mind—all!
This is what we are to aim at.

Not that we do not thank the Lord—I trust we do—but that it may be more spiritual in character, that the heart may be engaged more and more, and all that is within us be occupied with praising, adoring, and magnifying the Lord.
Then there is a remarkable addition to this: “Bless His holy name.”
This is something only believers can be engaged in.
By nature, we do not care about the holiness of God.
By nature, man likes to gratify himself, and would have God be like himself.
By nature, the attribute of holiness is the last one we care about.
But when we are born again, when we are renewed, when we have spiritual life, a longing after holiness is begotten in our hearts, and we rejoice in the fact that God is a holy Being.
Then we have the prospect of one day being like Him.
Only a child of God takes a real interest in admiring the holiness of God and in rendering praise to Him for it.
Then the Psalmist adds, in the second verse: “Bless Jehovah, O my soul, and do not forget all His benefits.”
We are in danger of forgetting the mercies of God.

We are ready to speak about our trials, our difficulties, our bereavements, our crosses; but are we just as ready to speak of and admire the goodness of God, and His mercies bestowed on us in countless ways all the days of our life?
This was something the Psalmist was particularly concerned about.
Now to our text:
“Who forgives all your iniquities.”
This is the first blessing the Psalmist lists.
It is the first mercy he especially desired not to forget.
Notice particularly that among all the blessings this is the first.
And is this not the choicest blessing we have received?
Is there one single blessing to be compared with this?
What are all our blessings in business—and they are something to be grateful for—in comparison with the forgiveness of our sins?
What is all the peace and quietness in the family—and these too are something to be grateful for—compared with the forgiveness of our sins?
What is the soundness of bodily health—for which we should be thankful—in comparison with the forgiveness of our sins?
What is the vigor and strength of mind with which we are blessed, in comparison with the forgiveness of our sins?
It is as nothing in comparison with it.
The Psalmist puts this blessing first because it is the choicest, the chief, and the most precious a human being can have.
Let me ask affectionately: Have we all obtained the forgiveness of our sins?
That is the point! That is the point!
Are we all pardoned sinners?
We are all sinners, without exception.
Are we all pardoned sinners?
Have we all obtained the forgiveness of our sins?
That is the point!
I have no doubt many hundreds here have; but at the same time I cannot help feeling that there are many who have not.
Now this is the momentous point: To which of the two classes do we belong?
Pardoned sinners—sinners whose load of guilt has been removed; or unpardoned sinners, unable to look up to God peacefully and calmly through the atonement of the Lord Jesus Christ?
Ask yourselves before God: To which class do I belong?
If I am not pardoned, I am without peace; I cannot look forward peacefully and calmly to eternity, and I do not know what the end of my course will be.
It is a fearful thing to go on day by day unpardoned.
This leads to the question: How can we obtain the forgiveness of our sins?
Simply by laying hold, through faith, of the atonement of the Lord Jesus Christ.
God, in the riches of His grace, instead of sending us to the place of perdition as we deserved, laid all the punishment due for our countless transgressions on His Son, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Him He sent into the world, so that in our place and stead He might work out a righteousness for us by fulfilling the whole law of God; so that poor guilty sinners who trust in Him will be regarded by God as if they had lived the holy and spotless life of the Lord Jesus Christ.

The believing sinner, standing before God in the righteousness of Christ—hiding himself, as he does, in the righteousness of the Lord Jesus Christ worked out for the poor sinner who trusts in Him—is accepted by Him.
In our place the Lord Jesus Christ bore every particle of the punishment that we wicked, guilty sinners ought to have endured.

Now God looks to us, not to do something to complete the work of salvation, but to accept what He so graciously provides for the sinner in the person of His Son, whose righteousness He accepts for the sinner.
But when the sinner believes in the Lord Jesus Christ, a different life begins: he seeks to please Christ, he seeks to adorn His doctrine, he seeks to walk according to His mind.
He does this not to be saved by it, or to add to the work of the Lord Jesus Christ.
But having been saved through faith, having obtained forgiveness, and having been accepted in the righteousness of the Lord Jesus Christ worked out for sinners, he seeks to please God.
This is the way to obtain forgiveness—simply trusting in Jesus, and so believing in Jesus.
Whoever does this obtains forgiveness.
Another important point is the knowledge of our forgiveness.
We are not to wait for this knowledge until we die, much less are we to wait for it until the day of judgment.
The blessing is to be had now, is to be known now, is something to be enjoyed now.
He who is without it cannot be very happy for any length of time.
It is this which brings the peace and joy of the Holy Spirit into the heart—the knowledge that, wicked and guilty as we are, our sins are forgiven.
My beloved Christian friends, do we all enjoy the forgiveness of our sins?
I trust none of you say it cannot be had.
It certainly can. This was the blessing the first Christians enjoyed.
They knew in whom they believed: that in Him they had “redemption through His blood, even the forgiveness of sins.”
They had this statement set before them concerning the Lord Jesus Christ: “To Him all the prophets give witness, that through His name whoever believes in Him shall receive remission of sins.”
So every poor sinner who believes in Jesus obtains the forgiveness of sins.
This truly is a blessing to be had now.
If any of you are without this blessing, give the Lord no rest until you know that your sins are forgiven.
It truly is to be had and enjoyed now, for salvation brings present blessing with it.
This is one of the blessings connected with our believing in the Lord Jesus Christ—to obtain the knowledge of forgiveness.
Notice further the statement of the Psalmist: not “Who forgives some of your iniquities,” but ALL.
That is so precious.
It is not that five hundred of our sins are forgiven, or five thousand, but every one; so that though they are countless, every one is forgiven.
Just think—vile and guilty as we are, every sin of everyone who believes in the Lord Jesus Christ is forgiven.
Do you enjoy it?
I do enjoy the forgiveness of my sins.
Not because I have very strong feelings.
I do not rest on feelings.
I take God at His word.
I rest on His word: “Whoever believes in Him shall not perish, but have eternal life.”
I believe in Jesus; therefore I have been pardoned.
I have had no dream or vision about it.
Some people think that unless, by some strange vision or other, they see Jesus hanging on the cross in some corner of the room, they must remain in doubt.
I have had no such vision.
For fifty years I have never had a single minute’s doubt about the forgiveness of my sins.
For these years I have been a believer, and all this time the word I have referred to, and on which I rest, has been written in the Book, and by it I know my sins are forgiven.
Every believer who is willing to take God at His word has a right to regard himself as a pardoned sinner, as a forgiven sinner.
This is a blessing, a great blessing, to know that all our sins are forgiven.
Suppose now our sins were just 9,090, and suppose we had forgiveness for 9,089—just one single sin unforgiven.
What then? This one single sin would bring us to the place of perdition.
There is no trifling with sin.
We must be perfectly without sin—hiding ourselves in the merits of the Lord Jesus Christ, and fully pardoned—or we are unclean and cannot come into His presence.
Therefore see the blessedness of this statement of the Psalmist: “Who forgives ALL your iniquities.”
All gone! Oh, the blessedness of this!

Every one gone! Sins of action, sins of word, sins of thought, sins of feeling, sins of desire, sins of purpose, sins of inclination—all gone, as surely as we put our trust in the Lord Jesus Christ for the salvation of our souls.
Now comes a point to which I particularly wish to refer, for the instruction of Christians, and especially of young believers.
We read, “Who FORGIVES.”
This shows that forgiveness is something going on now.

Christians may say: Sometimes we have statements in the New Testament as if our sins were all forgiven, and sometimes as if we needed to obtain forgiveness; and this passage, “Who forgives,” seems as if forgiveness were going on.
The explanation is this.

In the position in which we stand as sinners—being by nature guilty criminals—the moment we believe in the Lord Jesus Christ we obtain the forgiveness of all our sins; and in the matter of our salvation, the thing is done once for all.

But then we pass out of the old relationship of guilty criminals toward the righteous Judge into the position of children; and in this relationship of children, though the matter of our salvation is settled, yet in that relationship of children, whenever we fail—as is more or less the case day by day—and the Holy Spirit makes us conscious of our failure, we have to own before God, in childlike simplicity, that in such a way we have not behaved ourselves, that we have left this thing undone, or that we have done that thing improperly.

In childlike simplicity we are to make confession before the Lord; then that word comes in: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness”; and there is a necessity for the High-Priestly office of the Lord Jesus Christ.

As far as the matter of our salvation is concerned, when He died He could say, “It is finished”; and He then ascended as the great High Priest, still to point, on the sinner’s behalf, to the efficacy of His blood.

It is in this latter sense—in our position as children—that we need to make confession whenever we err or fail, to obtain the Fatherly forgiveness granted us; and this will be ours as surely as we confess. I trust this will serve as the explanation for my dear Christian friends.
“Who heals all your diseases.”
This is the next blessing the Psalmist desired to keep in mind.

Here we do not mean to say that the diseases of the body are excluded; for if anyone is cured of any bodily disease, it is not by the skill of the doctor, or by the powerful nature of the medicine, but by the blessing of God on the skill of the doctor.
Still, I judge that the special point referred to here is spiritual disease.
You remember what Isaiah said at the beginning of his prophecies: “From the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness, but wounds, and bruises, and putrefying sores.”
We all know that this did not refer to the bodies of the Israelites—that they were not in that loathsome state as regards the body—but that the reference was to their spiritual diseases.
That is the case with all sinners, at all times, and under all circumstances.
If we are spiritually pure, it must come from the Lord.

Now we have particularly to remember here that the poor sinner who trusts in the Lord Jesus Christ, the moment he does so, is, as it were unconsciously, putting himself under the infinitely wise and gracious Physician.
That blessed One takes him up and puts him into His own hospital, His own infirmary, and will not let him go until he is perfectly cured.

And as you all know, there is no such thing as a discharge from that hospital or infirmary on account of incurable disease, as is commonly the case among men; but the patient is cared for until he is perfectly free from spiritual disease.
The moment we are there, the cure is going on.
This very meeting is intended, by the blessing of Jesus, to do something toward that cure, to help us out of the diseased state.

And this is the prospect of the weakest: that as surely as he believes in Jesus, as surely as he is not willfully living in sin, so surely will he finally be brought into that state in which he will be altogether free from sin.
We have been laid hold of by God to be conformed to the image of His Son, to be at last altogether like Him, altogether holy, altogether free from spiritual disease.
Pride will be completely gone; irritability, covetousness, worldly-mindedness will all be gone.
We shall be gentle and lovely, pure and holy—just like Jesus.
Oh, the blessed prospect, that Jesus will not give us up until we are altogether free from our spiritual diseases!
Then this will be fulfilled: “Who heals all your diseases.”
Such is His discipline and care that day by day something will be done toward this complete cure; and we should say to ourselves, Have I made some progress today?
Am I a little freer from disease today than I was yesterday?
Am I somewhat more conformed to Jesus today?

At the new year we should say, Have I made more progress during the last year than in the previous one? For the will of the Lord concerning us is that we should be like Jesus at the last; and that the will of God should only need to be presented to us, and instantly, in our inmost souls, we should be ready to do it.
The Psalmist desired to be grateful to God that He was carrying on this cure.
“Who redeems your life from destruction.”
This is true in a variety of ways.
As regards natural life: If God did not watch over us, what would become of us?
We are constantly exposed to the loss of our life.
This is particularly so in the case of little children.
When you look at the little children by the dozen in the neighborhood of the Tabernacle, and the carts and carriages going by, who does not see that God watches over them?
How true as to natural life: “Who redeems your life from destruction.”
Then when we go on a journey, how exposed our life is to danger.
And even if we go on no journey, but lie on our beds, we are continually exposed to the loss of our life.
How often a stack of chimneys has fallen, and people have been crushed instantly!
But there is more in it than this.
Our whole life was to be for the glory of God.
Now, unless we had believed in Jesus—either as the Messiah who was to come, or in Him who had come—this life given to us would have been spent in hell.
Our life has indeed been redeemed from destruction.
But as regards those who are not yet believers in the Lord Jesus Christ, their life, given to them for the glory of Christ and to be enjoyed throughout eternity, is still liable to be spent in hell.
See to it that your life is redeemed from destruction; for unless you are a believer in the Lord Jesus Christ, it is not yet fully true that your life is redeemed from destruction.
Further: we who are believers in the Lord Jesus Christ, who desire to live for Christ—suppose we had been left to ourselves since we believed—we would have gone back.
We owe it to the grace and mercy and faithfulness of God that we are on the Lord’s side this day, and that we have not gone back again into the world.

Therefore, how deeply important it is to feel grateful that we have been upheld, and that we have the word, “He who has begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ,” and that He will never leave us nor forsake us.
How blessed, how glorious this prospect is!
“Who crowns you with lovingkindness and tender mercies.”
This was the next mercy for which the Psalmist desired to be especially grateful.
We should have a clear understanding of the figure used here.
Whenever a figure is used in the Scriptures, we should seek to understand it clearly, so as to be able to know the meaning of the spiritual truth expressed under it.
The figure here is “crowning.”

We all know, with regard to crowning, that not a dozen persons in a country are crowned, nor half a dozen, but that one individual is singled out, on whose head the crown is placed as a mark of honor and power.
But this individual, singled out and taken from among the rest, is placed in this position of honor and power by the crown put on his head.
Precisely so our heavenly Father deals with us who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ; we are not a particle better than the vilest.
We are just as wicked as the poor prisoners on the Cut, or in the Bridewell, or at Lawford’s Gate.
In ourselves we are just as bad as they are, just as bad as the vilest in the city.
When we see drunkards or prisoners being carried off by the police officers, we should say, But for the grace of God I would now be a drunkard.
But for the grace of God I would be in the hands of those policemen.

And this we should never lose sight of to the last, so that the heart may be filled with love and gratitude to God more and more, and to the Lord Jesus Christ more and more, more and more; for had we been left to ourselves we would have been wallowing in sin, and in a far worse state.
And it is this particular point to which the Psalmist refers when he says, “Crowns you with lovingkindness and tender mercies”—lovingkindness meaning grace.
In the Old Testament, going to the Hebrew, it means grace.
It is to the grace and mercy of God that we are indebted.
But for the grace and mercy of God we would be like the vilest of the vile.

All this we should keep in mind, to keep us from high-mindedness and from thinking ourselves better than others, and so that the heart may remain filled with love and gratitude to the Lord Jesus Christ.
Now there is one more mercy remaining for which the Psalmist desired to be grateful.
Precious Lord Jesus Christ, use the mouth of Your servant now; by Your Spirit direct Your poor servant to bring out those very points which the beloved disciples especially need to help them.
Help Your servant, and let the Word come, not in word only but in the power of the Holy Spirit, so that it will not be forgotten to the end of the life of these dear disciples here.
And Your servant asks it for Your dear name’s sake.
“Who satisfies your mouth with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.”
Notice the figure again—the old eagles casting their feathers; and when this has been done, their strength is truly renewed, and they become strong and powerful again.
This was the case with those advanced in years.
So the Psalmist, looking at himself, admired what the Lord had done for him.
He does not refer to food, though that is included; and for every crumb of bread and drop of water we should be exceedingly grateful, for the body is strong and vigorous through the food given us.
The Psalmist meant to say that his mouth was satisfied with good things, as the eagle’s was, by means of good food.
But more than this: he was referring to spiritual food, through which his spiritual strength was renewed.
Now, beloved Christian friends, this is the momentous point.
There is no necessity for aged believers to become more and more lifeless and careless and worldly-minded.
As the Psalmist grew old he did not become very worldly-minded, he did not become lifeless and cold and carnal, but his spiritual strength was renewed.
So it may be with us.

It is a mistake to suppose that for two or three years after conversion we may be in a healthy and lively state, and that after we have known the Lord five or ten years we may expect to become cold and dead and formal, and to go back again little by little.
It may be far otherwise, it ought to be far otherwise; and if it is not, we are not living to the praise and glory of God.
The Psalmist in his advanced years was happier in the Lord, more spiritually minded; he had more spiritual power and vigor at the end than he had at the beginning.
Oh, my beloved younger brothers and sisters, you have before you not the prospect of dull and miserable days, but of brighter and happier days.
And here, for the honor and glory of God, I bear my own testimony.

I am happier now, after being a believer for nearly fifty-one years, than I was fifty years ago; far happier than I was forty years ago, than I was thirty years ago, than I was twenty years ago, than I was ten years ago.
As time has gone on, my peace and joy and happiness in the Lord have increased more and more, instead of fading away more and more.
Why do I refer to this?
Not to boast, for it is all by the grace of God, but to encourage my younger fellow believers to expect greater things from the Lord, who delights in giving abundantly.
And as you sometimes sing, “More and more, more and more,” there is yet more to come.
Let us look out for it, for God delights to give more grace.
It is the joy and delight of His heart to give more and more.
Why should it not be so?
Why should we not have the best things in the last part of life?
Has God changed? Far from it!
Has the Bible changed?
No! We have the same blessed word.
Is the power of the Holy Spirit less?
Far from it; nothing of the kind!
The Lord Jesus Christ is always ready to bless.
The word we now have is the whole revelation.
And our heavenly Father has the same heart toward His children.
Therefore there is nothing to hinder our being happier as time goes on with us.
If we are not happier, what is the reason?
There must be a reason, and we should ask ourselves why we are not getting happier and happier.
Now, in brotherly love and affection, I would give a few hints to my younger fellow believers as to the way to keep up spiritual enjoyment.
It is absolutely necessary, in order that happiness in the Lord may continue, that the Scriptures be read regularly.
They are God’s appointed means for the nourishment of the inner man.
If the Word of God is neglected, you are not making progress, but you are spiritual babes, and remain so.
That is not all.
You will become spiritual dwarfs! You will become spiritual dwarfs! Spiritual dwarfs!
Instead of living to the glory of God, you will be living to dishonor Him.
You see, we are left here after conversion to live for the benefit of the world.
Only a few of the children of God are taken to heaven directly after their conversion; the rest are left to live here for a while for the glory of God.
This cannot be unless we regularly give ourselves to the Word of God, unless we come to it day by day and pray over it.
We should consider it and ponder over it in reference to our own needs.
But especially we should read regularly through the Scriptures, consecutively, and not pick out a chapter here and there.
If we do, we remain spiritual dwarfs.
I tell you so affectionately.
For the first four years after my conversion I made no progress, because I neglected the Bible.
But when I regularly read on through the whole of it with reference to my own heart and soul, I made progress immediately.
Then my peace and joy continued more and more.
Now I have been doing this for forty-seven years.
I have read through the whole Bible about one hundred times, and I always find it fresh when I begin it again.
So my peace and joy have increased more and more.
Now think of it, you beloved younger brothers and sisters in particular, and say, Let me live to the glory of God.

And if you have reached middle age and have neglected to read the Word of God in this way, begin it now with earnestness; and if you read it like this, with prayer and application to your own heart, and seek to practice what you find, your peace and joy will increase more and more, more and more; and it will be said of you, “Your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.”
How bright, then, are the prospects of eternity when we lay hold of the precious Word!
May the Lord grant that we may each be able to do so!
But are there any dear friends here who have not yet obtained forgiveness?

If there are, let them now pass sentence on themselves, let them now condemn themselves as guilty sinners, and put their whole trust for salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom alone it is to be obtained.
And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men.
Truly I say to you, they have their reward.
But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.
But when you pray, do not use vain repetitions, as the heathen do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking.
Therefore do not be like them, for your Father knows the things you have need of before you ask Him.
In this manner, therefore, pray: Our Father who is in heaven, hallowed be Your name.
Your kingdom come. Your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.
Give us this day our daily bread.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For Yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen.
For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: but if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.—Matthew 6:5–15.

We will meditate on part of Matthew 6, beginning at verse 5: “When you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites are, for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men.
Truly, I say to you, they have their reward.”
With regard to not a few of the Pharisees of old, this was actually the case.

They would stand praying for a long time in the synagogues; but what was far worse than this, when the ordinary time of prayer came for the Israelites—about three o’clock in the afternoon by our time—they would so arrange it that at that very time they could be found at the corners of the streets, where they might be observed in the act of prayer by as many people as possible coming from different directions.
All this was hypocrisy.
In this way they professed to be very holy men, but in reality it was the reverse.
“Truly, I say to you, they have their reward.”
Their reward was the applause of their fellow men.
A poor, miserable recompense.
“But when you pray, go into your inner room.”
The great point here is secrecy with regard to prayer.
Not everyone is in such a position that they have a little room to which they can withdraw and lock the door.
But if it can be done, it should be done.
If it is impossible, God will accept us according to our position and circumstances.
I remember a case which I would like to relate, to show how people may be situated.
About fifty years ago I went to Germany to find missionaries for the East Indies.
On this journey I came to Magdeburg, one of the strongest and largest fortresses of the kingdom of Prussia.

There, in the house of a godly man in the army, I found a comrade of his, and since he lived in barracks, I said, “My dear brother, how do you manage with regard to prayer, since you are constantly surrounded by hundreds of soldiers?”
His reply was, “When I want to pray in secret, I go down into a large sand cellar, which is completely dark, and there I kneel down on the sand.
No one is able to see that I am there, though some of my comrades often come close on my heels; but I am never found there.
I am alone, completely alone; no one sees me; and that is my inner room.” So in whatever different ways the children of God may be situated, they have to do the best they can.

But the great point is that, as much as possible, we should seek to deal with our heavenly Father in prayer in secret, and under no circumstances aim to be noticed by our fellow men in order to gain their applause.
“When you pray, go into your inner room, and when you have shut your door” (thus further stating the exceedingly great importance of secrecy).
“Pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.”
Where there is this—a secret waiting on God—He, in His own time and way, will give the open recompense.
He will show that He is taking notice; He will show that He has recorded it in the book of remembrance; He will show that it has not escaped His observation.
“Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.”
The secret waiting on God will be made manifest by blessing.
As surely as we give ourselves to prayer in this way, God will take notice of us and give blessing that anyone can see.
“But when you pray, do not use vain repetitions, as the heathen do.”

That is, sentence after sentence repeating the same request, just as the worshipers of Baal did, and as the heathen nations do to the present time, thinking that the more their words, the more they repeat what they ask for, the more certain it is that they will get it.

“Do not use vain repetitions as the heathen do, for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking; therefore do not be like them, for your Father knows the things you have need of before you ask Him.”
Prayer is not necessary for the sake of informing God; but prayer is necessary simply because it is the appointment of God.

He would have us go to Him for our own good and profit and blessing, asking Him for the things we need, because the blessing given to us in answer to prayer is so much more precious than if the blessing were given without prayer.
Again and again God allows us to be greatly tried, in order that at last, when the blessing does come and prayer is answered, it may be all the more precious to us.
“Therefore do not be like them, for your Father knows the things you have need of before you ask Him.”
Now comes what is commonly called “The Lord’s Prayer.”
“In this manner, therefore, pray.”
This shows us that it is not God’s appointment that only these words of the Lord Jesus Christ should be used, nor that we should use them continually.
But in this spirit, in this manner, we should ask for blessing.
That is the lesson we have to learn.
“In this manner pray: ‘Our Father who is in heaven.’”
The very first word is full of meaning.
The petitions recorded here are suitable, and only suitable, for the children of God—for they are the prayer of the heavenly family, those who are believers in the Lord Jesus Christ.
We have to keep this before us: that as long as we are not believers in the Lord Jesus Christ, God is not our Father.
God is God to us.
He is our Creator.
He is our Preserver.
He is the One who supplies us with everything we can need.
He lets His sun shine for us; He also lets the rain fall, so that we benefit from it.
But until we are believers in the Lord Jesus Christ, God is not our Father.

Now this word “Our” shows that we are part of a family, part of the heavenly family; and so it is that all who put their trust in the Lord Jesus Christ for the salvation of their souls, after having been convinced that they are sinners deserving nothing but punishment—all such as are believers—have in God Almighty a Father.
“Who is in heaven.”
His place is everywhere, but it is especially in heaven, not on earth, though His power may be seen everywhere, and the manifestations of His presence may be found throughout the universe.
“Hallowed be Your Name.”
That is, may Your Name be honored; may Your Name be glorified.
And here I remind my beloved Christian friends of the meaning of the word “Name.”
It does not mean the several letters which form the name “God,” but what we learn in the thirty-fourth chapter of Exodus, when Jehovah proclaimed His Name before Moses.
It is His character, His attributes, what He is Himself, that are to be glorified.
Jehovah, the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of all those who believe in Jesus, is to be glorified.

That is the meaning of “Hallowed be Your Name”; and just in proportion as we enter into what God is, we find out what a lovely, lovely Being He is, how infinitely lovely He is. “Hallowed be Your Name.”
In other words, “I pray that You may be more and more honored and glorified.”
Now comes another petition.

“Your kingdom come.” That is, “Hasten the time, bring it about speedily, when You will be universally honored, when You will be universally glorified, when all the works of the wicked one will be destroyed.”
This will be after the return of the Lord Jesus Christ.
See how entirely impossible it is for the ungodly, the unconverted, to ask this petition from the heart.
The lips of such people may utter it countless times, but the true meaning is nothing short of this: “Let the time speedily come when I, a wicked creature, shall be cast into the bottomless pit.”
That is just the meaning of the prayer when it is uttered in this way; and of course this plainly shows that the ungodly could ask the petition “Your kingdom come” only in ignorance.
The words can only properly be used by those who are believers in the Lord Jesus, for they implore Him to return soon, so that God may be universally glorified and honored by everyone on earth.
That this is the meaning we see immediately from what follows.
“Your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.” Since the fall of Adam and Eve, the will of God has not been done on earth.

It was done in Paradise before the fall of Adam and Eve, but from the moment they ate of the forbidden fruit, and sin was brought onto the earth by the devil, from that moment the will of God was not done fully on earth, as it should be, and as it will be hereafter when the Lord Jesus Christ has returned.
Let us keep this clearly before us.
One of the first things that was done after the fall was that the first child of Adam and Eve, Cain, murdered his own brother, Abel.
There we see the fruit of sin entering into the world, and ever since then the will of God has not been “done on earth, as it is in heaven.”
There have been those who were godly in spirit, at various times, who have sought in their feeble measure to glorify God, and to walk to the praise and glory and honor of His Name.
But the great mass of human beings on earth have not been doing the will of God, as the will of God is done in heaven.
“Give us this day our daily bread.”
Here the daily bread does not mean simply bread and nothing else; it means the necessities of life in general.
What we need, we ask God for, and we are allowed to ask God to give it to us.
Notice particularly that it does not say here, “Give us our daily bread,” but “Give us this day our daily bread.”
That means we are not warranted to expect a great abundance in the way of supply of earthly things.

God may be going to fill our hearts with cause for gratitude; God may most abundantly give us the necessities of life beforehand, and a long time beforehand; but if He does not do it, we are not to blame Him, far less to consider that He is not faithful to His promise, for He has not promised that He will give us the necessities of life years beforehand, nor months beforehand, nor weeks beforehand, nor many days beforehand; He has only promised that day by day we shall be supplied, and this also only on the condition that we seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness.

In other words, if we walk in the fear of God, making it our business to win souls for Him and to set a good example of godly walk and behavior before our fellow men, we shall then, as surely as we trust in Him, be supplied with the necessities of life.
For so David said, “I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed”—that is, his children, his descendants—“begging bread.”
“Give us this day our daily bread.”
On this petition we may write clothes, house rent, taxes, supplies for everything our family requires.
All this is implied in the petition for daily bread.
And how precious it is to have to go to a loving Father, whose very joy and delight it is to answer the petitions of His children.
He is not a hard Master, an austere Being, but an infinitely loving Father.

Oh, that it might increasingly come to every one of the children of God to look at Him as an infinitely loving Being; for when we are brought to this state, we are perfectly satisfied at all times and under all circumstances with His dealings with us.
Whether they are painful or otherwise, we are satisfied that He does all things well.
“And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”
This implies acknowledging that we are sinners.

It is a matter of exceedingly great importance that we give ourselves to God as we are, not seeking to make out that we are very good people, very excellent people, that we habitually walk in His ways and act according to His mind—for the very reverse is the case, more or less, with every one of us, even the best among us.

Therefore we should increasingly acknowledge before God that we are sinners, that we have not acted at all times and under all circumstances according to His mind, and have accordingly contracted debts, spiritual debts, because we are transgressors.
We should acknowledge that we are debtors before God, and ask His forgiveness for Christ’s sake, seeking it in God’s appointed way, through Jesus.
